title: Test for continuity: fuses, switches, wires and elements
summary: Use the meter's continuity beeper or ohms range to find broken wires, blown fuses, dead switches, burnt-out heating elements and shorts. It is the most-used test in salvage and repair, and it only works on circuits that are switched off.

steps.text: Unplug or disconnect the power, and discharge any big capacitors. Continuity tests are for dead circuits only.
steps.warn: Testing continuity on a live circuit can wreck the meter and burn you.

steps.text: Set the meter to continuity (a sound-wave or diode symbol) or the lowest ohms range. Touch the probes together: it should beep and read close to 0 Ω. Note the reading; that is your lead resistance.
Isolate the part you are testing. Take a fuse out of its holder, or disconnect one end of a switch or element. Otherwise you may be measuring through other parts.
Fuses: a good fuse beeps and reads close to 0 Ω. OL means blown. Glass fuses often show a broken wire or a black smudge inside.
Switches: test across the terminals in each position. On should beep; off should read OL. A switch that crackles or reads several ohms when on is worn.
Wires and cords: test each wire from end to end. Bend the cable along its length while testing. A beep that cuts in and out means broken strands, often near a plug.
Shorts: test between every pair of wires, and from each wire to any metal case. They should read OL.
steps.warn: A cord or appliance with continuity from live or neutral to its metal case can give a shock. Don't use it.

steps.text: Heating elements: measure ohms. Most read a few to a few tens of ohms. OL means burnt out. Expected resistance is about volts × volts ÷ watts.
Thermal fuses and bimetal thermostats: good thermal fuses read close to 0 Ω. Most heating thermostats read close to 0 Ω at room temperature.
Mark what you have tested with tape: OK or BAD.

notes:
## What the readings mean

| Reading | Means |
|---|---|
| Beep, about 0–1 Ω | Good connection |
| A few ohms to kilohms | Something is in the path: a winding, an element, a resistor, or a poor contact |
| OL (or a 1 on the left on older meters) | Open: no connection |

Most meters beep for anything under roughly 30–50 Ω, so a beep doesn't prove a perfect connection. Read the number too.

## Element resistance worked out

Resistance ≈ volts × volts ÷ watts.

- 230 V, 2,000 W kettle element: 230 × 230 ÷ 2,000 ≈ 26 Ω.
- 120 V, 1,500 W heater element: 120 × 120 ÷ 1,500 ≈ 9.6 Ω.

Readings close to these mean the element is good.

## Holding the probes

On high ohms ranges your body adds a reading. Don't hold both metal tips with your fingers. Use clips, or hold only one end.

## Common mistakes

- Testing in circuit and getting a false path through other parts.
- Testing a circuit that is still live.
- Forgetting to subtract lead resistance on low readings.
- Assuming a beep means a wire can carry heavy current. One strand left in a frayed cable still beeps.
